cells.tense: You're at the bench and the work is in your hands, cut and measured, nothing left pretending.
cells.ask: Let one thing you've guided past its finish be finished, and stand there a moment without picking up the next.
cells.core:
You know how to set a thing down when it's done. You've held something long enough to know what it cost, you've ended it anyway, and what you kept after was the part that mattered. That's steering, and it doesn't have to look dramatic from outside.

What's free to grow here is the version of this that doesn't push — tending something on its own schedule, checking on it without gripping the outcome. Let one finished thing rest and don't fill the space in the same breath. What that leaves is a hand free to notice what's already coming up, and that's a real trade.
cells.sheetLine: You end what you mean to end, and the ending is clean.
cells.verb: ending a chosen thing on purpose, with full awareness of what it costs
cells.place: in the part of a life where you decide what you're actually pointed at

cells.tense: You're living a few steps ahead of where you are, rehearsing a finish that hasn't been given to you yet.
cells.ask: Pick one open thing and write down the conditions under which it would actually be done — then close the page for today.
cells.core:
You can see the end of everything you've started, so you're ending things before they've had a chance to be what they are. Tomorrow's finishing has moved into today, and you're steering from inside a version of events nobody else can see yet. People feel the push before they feel you.

Some of that grip is holding something together that matters to you, and it's a real thing to protect. But practice is what tells you a method is working — steady, unhurried, and the unhurried part is the point. Write the finish line for one open thing and leave it there. Quietly, the doing teaches you something the rehearsal can't.
cells.sheetLine: You decide what ends before it's begun, and the deciding costs the living.
cells.verb: ending a chosen thing on purpose, with full awareness of what it costs

cells.tense: You're still standing where a decision was already made, not yet come into the rest of the room.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you'd end if you were the one deciding, and read it back once without acting.
cells.core:
You steer when pushed, but left alone you don't come down on one side. Things stay half-ended and half-held, and the not-deciding gets called patience. Someone else's hand has been on the wheel and the door it closed is behind you, not in front.

What steadies this is finding out you can carry a weight without forcing anyone under it — that strength isn't the same as pressure. The move back into your own hands is small and physical: write one ending you'd choose if the call were yours, read it, put the pen down. Just having said it once is a load the body can feel.

cells.tense: You're driving and describing it as being driven, the pen's fallen out of your hand while you sit at the desk.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been ending on purpose anyway, just by how you spend your hours.
cells.core:
You steer better than you give yourself credit for. When you choose what you're pointed at, the week arranges itself around that choice — you show up early, the small stuff falls away, and the people around you feel the difference in how you hold a room. That's steadying, and it's the part you skip past.

What's been happening quietly is the same act, one ending at a time — the calls you let go, the things you stopped pursuing, the space you stopped giving. You file it as life happening. It's smaller to tend something ordinary and let it grow on its own, without forcing the shape. Say which ending is yours, out loud, and that answer stops belonging to anyone but you.
cells.sheetLine: You've been deciding what ends. That decision is yours.
